<translation>
<pb n="224"/>teachings for the purpose of scripture, for the purpose of comprehension, and for the purpose of following the instructions. "Great Being" <note>original: Mahasattva</note> should be understood in three aspects of greatness: great armor, great engagement, and great noble ascent. In that regard, "armor" refers to making aspirations. "Engagement" refers to entering that great enlightenment. "Noble ascent" refers to this "purifying the path of the Noble Bodhisattva," which shows how they have reached the ultimate perfection. This is a "gate of Dharma" <note>original: dharmamukha</note>, and it is also the "illumination of other gates of Dharma," because through it all the meanings of the Great Vehicle appear; thus it is the illumination of the gate of Dharma. One should understand the "gate of Dharma" to be the enumeration of the Dharma. "Ultimate perfection" is so called because it transcends all phenomena and is supreme. That which is called the "presentation of the classifications" shows that the enumeration of the Dharma is to be known through worldly knowledge. That which is called "this place of knowing the presentation is inconceivable" shows that here it is the supra-mundane primordial wisdom. If one asks what is fully shown by this: it shows that by the mere presentation of the classifications of the levels, one should understand that this is not yet the actual purification of the Bodhisattva levels.

Then the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having uttered merely the names of those ten levels of the Bodhisattva, sat in silence without further explaining them in detail. Then the entire assembly of Bodhisattvas, having heard merely the names of those ten levels of the Bodhisattva but not hearing the detailed classifications of the levels described, became thirsty for the teaching and thought to themselves: why is it that the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having uttered merely the names of those ten levels of the Bodhisattva, sits in silence, letting the time pass without showing them further in detail? What is the cause and what is the condition for this? At that time, in that gathered assembly of Bodhisattvas, there sat a Bodhisattva, a Great Being named Vimukticandra <note>Moon of Liberation</note>. Then the Bodhisattva 

<pb n="225"/>Vimukticandra, having fully known the thoughts and intentions of that assembly of Bodhisattvas, questioned the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in melodic verses:

You whose thoughts are fully purified,
Endowed with mindfulness, wisdom, and virtues,
Having spoken of the supreme levels,
O All-Pervading Lord, why do you not explain them?
All these here are of certain resolve,
These Bodhisattvas of great renown;
Why, after naming the levels,
Do you not explain their classifications?
All these sons of the Conqueror
Are fearless and desire to hear;
The manner of the meaning of the levels,
Please explain them in detail.
This assembly is very pure,
Free from laziness, beautiful and noble,
Abiding firmly in the essence of purity,
Fully endowed with virtue and wisdom.
All remain with great respect,
Looking at one another;
Like bees seeking honey and nectar,
They desire what should not be abandoned.

If one asks why he would remain silent: the Bodhisattvas hold the Dharma in high esteem, so he acts to make the Dharma esteemed by being urged by those who have become thirsty for it. Why did Vimukticandra initiate the urging first? Because he is the leader of that assembly, and so that the others would not fall into idle talk, and so that the assembly would remain gathered. Why use only melodic verses? To condense many meanings into few words, and because praises are mostly done in verse. If one asks what is fully shown by these five verses: it shows the absence of faults in the speaker and the listeners that would make them unworthy of the explanation. In that regard, the absence of faults in the speaker is shown by the phrase, "You whose thoughts are fully purified." The listeners who are compatible with the Dharma are so because of their certain resolve and their desire to hear. Others are so because their minds are very clear. To show that there is not a single person among them who is unworthy or unknown, he said: "All remain with great respect, looking at one another."

<pb n="226"/>Regarding that, the text of the verses spoken from his mouth is mostly for the sake of those who are weary; whichever text allows those who know it to focus on that meaning is the text itself. In the phrase, "You whose thoughts are fully purified, endowed with mindfulness, wisdom, and virtues, having spoken of the supreme levels, O All-Pervading Lord, why do you not explain them?" if one asks why it is shown by the purification of thoughts: it is because thoughts are the cause of explanation. "Thoughts" <note>original: samkalpa</note> are conceptualizations <note>original: vikalpa</note>; they are what perform the action. Therefore, if the cause of the explanation is purified, he requests: "Why do you not speak?" That purification of thought is also distinguished by two things: the adoption of the remedy and being free from faults. In that regard, being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom shows the adoption of the remedy for the afflicted thoughts and the perceptions arising from that basis. The applications of mindfulness are the remedy for afflicted thoughts; these are shown by the mention of "mindfulness." The wisdom that perceives Suchness is the remedy for the perceptions arising from that basis because it is signless; this is shown by the mention of "wisdom." The remaining words show the absence of faults. Regarding that, the faults that would prevent one from explaining are of three types: jealousy, stinginess, laziness when teaching the Dharma, and lack of confidence. In that regard, jealousy is not tolerating the knowledge of others. Stinginess is the mind's grasping. By being "endowed with virtues," it shows the absence of the first fault by possessing virtues such as lack of anger. By "having spoken of the levels," it shows the absence of the second fault. By "All-Pervading Lord," it shows the absence of the third fault. Thus, having praised the speaker with the two types of pure thought, he begins the praise of the listeners: "All these here are of certain resolve, these Bodhisattvas of great renown; why, after naming the levels, do you not explain their classifications?"

<pb n="227"/>"Certain resolve" means they are wise, with purified intellects. That certain resolve should be understood in three ways: certain resolve in the vast by making aspirations for great enlightenment, certain resolve in renown by being trusted by others in that same way, and certain resolve in being fully grasped by having comprehended it themselves from the speaker. These are shown respectively by the terms "Bodhisattva," "endowed with great renown," and "naming the levels." Even if one has certain resolve, if one does not seek the meaning, one is not a vessel for the explanation; therefore, he said: "All these sons of the Conqueror are desiring to hear." There is certain resolve regarding the scripture, but there may not be certain resolve regarding the realization, and the meaning may be hidden; if the meaning were not hidden, the vessel for the explanation would not be fully perfected. Therefore, to show both, he said: "fearless." Seeing the Dharma and the meaning not being hidden results in being fearless. Therefore, knowing those vessels to be fully perfected, he urges them: "The manner of the meaning of the levels, please explain them in detail." Thus, having praised the compatible assembly with the two virtues of certain resolve and seeking the meaning, he praises the others: "This assembly is very pure, free from laziness, beautiful and noble, abiding firmly in the essence of purity, fully endowed with virtue and wisdom." In that regard, "very pure" means clean, not turbid. Regarding that, if absent, there are six types of turbidity that make it very pure: the turbidity of not seeking the meaning, the turbidity of conduct, the turbidity of obscuration, seeking faults, the turbidity of intention by having the intention to be freed from such a debate, and not delighting in whatever is explained. Not being stable because of not being grounded in the roots of virtue is the turbidity of instability; the turbidity of delusion caused by being foolish and so forth.

<pb n="228"/>One should understand that there are six types of lack of turbidity as the remedies for those. In that regard, "abiding firmly in the essence" means making practice the essence of this teaching. The six phrases—"free from laziness," "beautiful and noble," "pure," "abiding firmly in the essence," "endowed with virtue," and "endowed with wisdom"—show those respectively. Thus, with two verses, he showed the purity of his own kind. Having shown the purity of other kinds with one, the purity of their mutual looking at each other is shown: "All remain with great respect, looking at one another." In that regard, the phrase "with great respect" shows that the mutual looking is not afflicted; it is done out of respect for the Dharma and not out of jealousy. "Like bees seeking honey and nectar, they desire what should not be abandoned," shows the supremacy of that very respect, as it is not a looking out of social obligation. In this verse, "looking at one another" is the primary limb. "The mutual looking not being afflicted" is the secondary limb. One should understand for the others as well that the first is the limb and the remainder are the secondary limbs. The similarity of characteristics, the difference of characteristics, and the summary and expansion are as before. In this verse, "Vajragarbha, of great wisdom and fearlessness, having heard that, spoke to the sons of the Sugata in order to make the assembly rejoice," speaking to make the assembly rejoice is the limb, which is the characteristic of making them understand. That making them understand is also of two types: making them understand through knowledge and making them understand through lack of discouragement. These are shown by "great wisdom" and "fearlessness." Without the first, one cannot make others understand. Without the second, the act of making them understand will not be made clear. Both are shown because of having fully abandoned the faults of the mental continuums of oneself and others. What is that making them understand?

<pb n="229"/>It is the fact that this Dharma is difficult to explain and difficult to hear. To show that it is difficult to explain, he said: "This is the supreme and marvelous difficulty, the fully revealed conduct of the Bodhisattvas, the supreme classification of the grounds and causes, from which the state of a Buddha is truly obtained." In that regard, "difficulty" means difficult to accomplish. There are two types of difficulty: the difficulty of extreme hardship and the difficulty of unfamiliarity. These are shown by "supreme" and "marvelous." If one asks why it is so difficult: "The fully revealed conduct of the Bodhisattvas, the supreme classification of the grounds and causes." In that regard, the "conduct of the Bodhisattvas" is the primordial wisdom of realization. Because it fully shows that, it is "fully revealed." "The supreme classification of the grounds and causes" means that the teaching of the levels, which are the causes of the Bodhisattva's conduct, is the ultimate perfection. What is the conduct of the Bodhisattvas like? He said: "From which the state of a Buddha is truly obtained." The "state of a Buddha" is Buddhahood itself, the primordial wisdom of a Buddha. Having shown the difficulty of explaining, he shows the cause of why it is difficult. What is its cause? It is that the meaning of the Bodhisattva's conduct cannot be explained exactly as it exists. If one asks how that meaning exists: "Fine in parts, difficult to see, abandoning conceptualization; because it is free from the ground of the mind, it is difficult to accomplish. It is the untainted sphere of the wise; if the world hears it, they will be deluded by it." In that regard, "difficulty of accomplishment" is the limb. The rest are secondary limbs. Regarding that, "difficult to accomplish" means difficult to obtain, which means difficult to realize. That difficulty of accomplishment is of four types, from "difficult to accomplish because it is fine in parts" up to "difficult to accomplish because it is free from the ground of the mind." In that regard, "fine in parts" means it is not something to be known by wisdom arising from hearing, for the coarse is not something to be known without needing contemplation. "Difficult to see"

<pb n="230"/>means it is not something to be known even by what arises from contemplation. "Abandoning conceptualization" means it is not something to be known even by what arises from worldly meditation, because conceptualizations are the minds and mental factors of the three realms. This shows, for the time being, that it is not the sphere of knowledge arising from worldly application. By the phrase "free from the ground of the mind," it shows that it is also not the sphere of the specific minds arising from the maturation of what is obtained at birth; here, the "ground of the mind" should be taken as the sphere of the mind. If so, whose sphere is it? He said: "It is the untainted sphere of the wise," which means the sphere of those who have seen the truth. Why not for others? Because it is "untainted," which means supra-mundane. Therefore, it is not something to be known by worldly knowledge. Thus, even if one explains that profound meaning as best as one can, it is difficult; as he said: "If the world hears it, they will be deluded by it." How are they deluded? By grasping the meaning according to the literal sound. "If they hear" means that for those who hear it, the difficulty of explaining is of that nature. Now, as for how it is difficult to hear: "Having established the intention to be like a diamond, being deeply devoted to the supreme wisdom of the Buddha, and having realized the selflessness of the ground of the mind, one can hear this very fine part of primordial wisdom." In that regard, "like a diamond" means having made it firm like a diamond. Firmness is of two types: firmness of devotion and firmness of realization; these are shown by three phrases. In that regard, "firmness" is the limb. The rest are secondary limbs. What is the devotion to the supreme wisdom of the Buddha like? The enlightenment of a Buddha is infinite; one should think with the mind of devotion and faith: "Regarding sentient beings, the Thus-Gone Ones engage in teaching the Dharma of the Thus-Gone Ones; therefore the Buddha himself knows, but I do not." What is the ground of the mind? How does one realize

<pb n="231"/>selflessness in it? The "ground of the mind" is the three realms where the mind matures and wherever that mind moves by focusing on all phenomena. In both of those aspects, it is realizing the selflessness of persons and phenomena exactly as they truly are. "Very fine" means very difficult to realize; how it is fine was shown previously. Now it is shown by mentioning examples: "Just as a painting is drawn in the sky, and just as the wind stays in the expanse of space, so too here, the untainted primordial wisdom of the Blessed Ones is difficult to see when classified." This shows the following: for example, a painting drawn in the sky is not visible because it does not abide there as it does on a wall; and for example, the wind in the sky is not visible through its moving activity because it does not abide there like a leaf; yet it is not that those two do not occur in the sky. Likewise, the explanation, which is like the wind, and the drawing of a painting on the inexpressible reality, which is like the sky, are not visible because they are not of that nature; because they arise suddenly and do not abide there. However, it is not that they do not occur there. Thus, the primordial wisdom of the Buddha is divided into parts by the classifications of the explanation; although classified, it is difficult to see. In that regard, the drawing of the painting shows the collections of names, phrases, and letters, because it is the occasion of the explanation. The wind, which is the basis of sound, shows the words; those two are what is to be explained and what is to be heard. If one asks, "If it can be heard in any way, why not explain it even if it is difficult to see?" he said: "My mind thinks this: Who in the world will realize this? Since one who is clear-minded in this supreme matter is rare, I have no joy in explaining this." In that regard, "to realize" means to comprehend. "Clear-minded" means endowed with devotion. What does this show? If those endowed with the previously mentioned realization and devotion can hear this, they are rare in the world; therefore, he thinks, "I will not speak."
</translation>

<summary>This passage continues the dialogue between the Bodhisattvas Vajragarbha and Vimukticandra, explaining the profound difficulty of teaching and comprehending the ten Bodhisattva levels. It uses metaphors like paintings in the sky to illustrate how the Buddha's untainted wisdom, while classifiable through words, remains beyond worldly conceptualization.</summary>

<keywords>Vajragarbha, Vimukticandra, ten levels, bhumi, primordial wisdom, jnana, selflessness, devotion, dharmamukha, Great Vehicle</keywords>

"Great Being" <note>original: Mahasattva</note> should be understood in three aspects of greatness: great armor, great engagement, and great noble ascent. In that regard, "armor" refers to making aspirations. "Engagement" refers to entering that great enlightenment. "Noble ascent" refers to this "purifying the path of the Noble Bodhisattva," which shows how they have reached the ultimate perfection. This is a "gate of Dharma" <note>original: dharmamukha</note>, and it is also the "illumination of other gates of Dharma," because through it all the meanings of the Great Vehicle appear; thus it is the illumination of the gate of Dharma. One should understand the "gate of Dharma" to be the enumeration of the Dharma. "Ultimate perfection" is so called because it transcends all phenomena and is supreme. That which is called the "presentation of the classifications" shows that the enumeration of the Dharma is to be known through worldly knowledge. That which is called "this place of knowing the presentation is inconceivable" shows that here it is the supra-mundane primordial wisdom. If one asks what is fully shown by this: it shows that by the mere presentation of the classifications of the levels, one should understand that this is not yet the actual purification of the Bodhisattva levels.

Then the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having uttered merely the names of those ten levels of the Bodhisattva, sat in silence without further explaining them in detail. Then the entire assembly of Bodhisattvas, having heard merely the names of those ten levels of the Bodhisattva but not hearing the detailed classifications of the levels described, became thirsty for the teaching and thought to themselves: why is it that the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, having uttered merely the names of those ten levels of the Bodhisattva, sits in silence, letting the time pass without showing them further in detail? What is the cause and what is the condition for this? At that time, in that gathered assembly of Bodhisattvas, there sat a Bodhisattva, a Great Being named Vimukticandra <note>Moon of Liberation</note>. Then the Bodhisattva
pages.tail: Vimukticandra, having fully known the thoughts and intentions of that assembly of Bodhisattvas, questioned the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in melodic verses:

pages.span:
Vimukticandra, having fully known the thoughts and intentions of that assembly of Bodhisattvas, questioned the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha in melodic verses:

You whose thoughts are fully purified,
Endowed with mindfulness, wisdom, and virtues,
Having spoken of the supreme levels,
O All-Pervading Lord, why do you not explain them?
All these here are of certain resolve,
These Bodhisattvas of great renown;
Why, after naming the levels,
Do you not explain their classifications?
All these sons of the Conqueror
Are fearless and desire to hear;
The manner of the meaning of the levels,
Please explain them in detail.
This assembly is very pure,
Free from laziness, beautiful and noble,
Abiding firmly in the essence of purity,
Fully endowed with virtue and wisdom.
All remain with great respect,
Looking at one another;
Like bees seeking honey and nectar,
They desire what should not be abandoned.

If one asks why he would remain silent: the Bodhisattvas hold the Dharma in high esteem, so he acts to make the Dharma esteemed by being urged by those who have become thirsty for it. Why did Vimukticandra initiate the urging first? Because he is the leader of that assembly, and so that the others would not fall into idle talk, and so that the assembly would remain gathered. Why use only melodic verses? To condense many meanings into few words, and because praises are mostly done in verse. If one asks what is fully shown by these five verses: it shows the absence of faults in the speaker and the listeners that would make them unworthy of the explanation. In that regard, the absence of faults in the speaker is shown by the phrase, "You whose thoughts are fully purified." The listeners who are compatible with the Dharma are so because of their certain resolve and their desire to hear. Others are so because their minds are very clear. To show that there is not a single person among them who is unworthy or unknown, he said: "All remain with great respect, looking at one another."
pages.head: Then the Bodhisattva

pages.span: Regarding that, the text of the verses spoken from his mouth is mostly for the sake of those who are weary; whichever text allows those who know it to focus on that meaning is the text itself. In the phrase, "You whose thoughts are fully purified, endowed with mindfulness, wisdom, and virtues, having spoken of the supreme levels, O All-Pervading Lord, why do you not explain them?" if one asks why it is shown by the purification of thoughts: it is because thoughts are the cause of explanation. "Thoughts" <note>original: samkalpa</note> are conceptualizations <note>original: vikalpa</note>; they are what perform the action. Therefore, if the cause of the explanation is purified, he requests: "Why do you not speak?" That purification of thought is also distinguished by two things: the adoption of the remedy and being free from faults. In that regard, being endowed with mindfulness and wisdom shows the adoption of the remedy for the afflicted thoughts and the perceptions arising from that basis. The applications of mindfulness are the remedy for afflicted thoughts; these are shown by the mention of "mindfulness." The wisdom that perceives Suchness is the remedy for the perceptions arising from that basis because it is signless; this is shown by the mention of "wisdom." The remaining words show the absence of faults. Regarding that, the faults that would prevent one from explaining are of three types: jealousy, stinginess, laziness when teaching the Dharma, and lack of confidence. In that regard, jealousy is not tolerating the knowledge of others. Stinginess is the mind's grasping. By being "endowed with virtues," it shows the absence of the first fault by possessing virtues such as lack of anger. By "having spoken of the levels," it shows the absence of the second fault. By "All-Pervading Lord," it shows the absence of the third fault. Thus, having praised the speaker with the two types of pure thought, he begins the praise of the listeners: "All these here are of certain resolve, these Bodhisattvas of great renown; why, after naming the levels, do you not explain their classifications?"

"Certain resolve" means they are wise, with purified intellects. That certain resolve should be understood in three ways: certain resolve in the vast by making aspirations for great enlightenment, certain resolve in renown by being trusted by others in that same way, and certain resolve in being fully grasped by having comprehended it themselves from the speaker. These are shown respectively by the terms "Bodhisattva," "endowed with great renown," and "naming the levels." Even if one has certain resolve, if one does not seek the meaning, one is not a vessel for the explanation; therefore, he said: "All these sons of the Conqueror are desiring to hear." There is certain resolve regarding the scripture, but there may not be certain resolve regarding the realization, and the meaning may be hidden; if the meaning were not hidden, the vessel for the explanation would not be fully perfected. Therefore, to show both, he said: "fearless." Seeing the Dharma and the meaning not being hidden results in being fearless. Therefore, knowing those vessels to be fully perfected, he urges them: "The manner of the meaning of the levels, please explain them in detail." Thus, having praised the compatible assembly with the two virtues of certain resolve and seeking the meaning, he praises the others: "This assembly is very pure, free from laziness, beautiful and noble, abiding firmly in the essence of purity, fully endowed with virtue and wisdom." In that regard, "very pure" means clean, not turbid. Regarding that, if absent, there are six types of turbidity that make it very pure: the turbidity of not seeking the meaning, the turbidity of conduct, the turbidity of obscuration, seeking faults, the turbidity of intention by having the intention to be freed from such a debate, and not delighting in whatever is explained. Not being stable because of not being grounded in the roots of virtue is the turbidity of instability; the turbidity of delusion caused by being foolish and so forth.

One should understand that there are six types of lack of turbidity as the remedies for those. In that regard, "abiding firmly in the essence" means making practice the essence of this teaching. The six phrases—"free from laziness," "beautiful and noble," "pure," "abiding firmly in the essence," "endowed with virtue," and "endowed with wisdom"—show those respectively. Thus, with two verses, he showed the purity of his own kind. Having shown the purity of other kinds with one, the purity of their mutual looking at each other is shown: "All remain with great respect, looking at one another." In that regard, the phrase "with great respect" shows that the mutual looking is not afflicted; it is done out of respect for the Dharma and not out of jealousy. "Like bees seeking honey and nectar, they desire what should not be abandoned," shows the supremacy of that very respect, as it is not a looking out of social obligation. In this verse, "looking at one another" is the primary limb. "The mutual looking not being afflicted" is the secondary limb. One should understand for the others as well that the first is the limb and the remainder are the secondary limbs. The similarity of characteristics, the difference of characteristics, and the summary and expansion are as before. In this verse, "Vajragarbha, of great wisdom and fearlessness, having heard that, spoke to the sons of the Sugata in order to make the assembly rejoice," speaking to make the assembly rejoice is the limb, which is the characteristic of making them understand. That making them understand is also of two types: making them understand through knowledge and making them understand through lack of discouragement. These are shown by "great wisdom" and "fearlessness." Without the first, one cannot make others understand. Without the second, the act of making them understand will not be made clear. Both are shown because of having fully abandoned the faults of the mental continuums of oneself and others. What is that making them understand?

It is the fact that this Dharma is difficult to explain and difficult to hear. To show that it is difficult to explain, he said: "This is the supreme and marvelous difficulty, the fully revealed conduct of the Bodhisattvas, the supreme classification of the grounds and causes, from which the state of a Buddha is truly obtained." In that regard, "difficulty" means difficult to accomplish. There are two types of difficulty: the difficulty of extreme hardship and the difficulty of unfamiliarity. These are shown by "supreme" and "marvelous." If one asks why it is so difficult: "The fully revealed conduct of the Bodhisattvas, the supreme classification of the grounds and causes." In that regard, the "conduct of the Bodhisattvas" is the primordial wisdom of realization. Because it fully shows that, it is "fully revealed." "The supreme classification of the grounds and causes" means that the teaching of the levels, which are the causes of the Bodhisattva's conduct, is the ultimate perfection. What is the conduct of the Bodhisattvas like? He said: "From which the state of a Buddha is truly obtained." The "state of a Buddha" is Buddhahood itself, the primordial wisdom of a Buddha. Having shown the difficulty of explaining, he shows the cause of why it is difficult. What is its cause? It is that the meaning of the Bodhisattva's conduct cannot be explained exactly as it exists. If one asks how that meaning exists: "Fine in parts, difficult to see, abandoning conceptualization; because it is free from the ground of the mind, it is difficult to accomplish. It is the untainted sphere of the wise; if the world hears it, they will be deluded by it." In that regard, "difficulty of accomplishment" is the limb. The rest are secondary limbs. Regarding that, "difficult to accomplish" means difficult to obtain, which means difficult to realize. That difficulty of accomplishment is of four types, from "difficult to accomplish because it is fine in parts" up to "difficult to accomplish because it is free from the ground of the mind." In that regard, "fine in parts" means it is not something to be known by wisdom arising from hearing, for the coarse is not something to be known without needing contemplation. "Difficult to see"
pages.tail: means it is not something to be known even by what arises from contemplation.

pages.span: means it is not something to be known even by what arises from contemplation. "Abandoning conceptualization" means it is not something to be known even by what arises from worldly meditation, because conceptualizations are the minds and mental factors of the three realms. This shows, for the time being, that it is not the sphere of knowledge arising from worldly application. By the phrase "free from the ground of the mind," it shows that it is also not the sphere of the specific minds arising from the maturation of what is obtained at birth; here, the "ground of the mind" should be taken as the sphere of the mind. If so, whose sphere is it? He said: "It is the untainted sphere of the wise," which means the sphere of those who have seen the truth. Why not for others? Because it is "untainted," which means supra-mundane. Therefore, it is not something to be known by worldly knowledge. Thus, even if one explains that profound meaning as best as one can, it is difficult; as he said: "If the world hears it, they will be deluded by it." How are they deluded? By grasping the meaning according to the literal sound. "If they hear" means that for those who hear it, the difficulty of explaining is of that nature. Now, as for how it is difficult to hear: "Having established the intention to be like a diamond, being deeply devoted to the supreme wisdom of the Buddha, and having realized the selflessness of the ground of the mind, one can hear this very fine part of primordial wisdom." In that regard, "like a diamond" means having made it firm like a diamond. Firmness is of two types: firmness of devotion and firmness of realization; these are shown by three phrases. In that regard, "firmness" is the limb. The rest are secondary limbs. What is the devotion to the supreme wisdom of the Buddha like? The enlightenment of a Buddha is infinite; one should think with the mind of devotion and faith: "Regarding sentient beings, the Thus-Gone Ones engage in teaching the Dharma of the Thus-Gone Ones; therefore the Buddha himself knows, but I do not." What is the ground of the mind? How does one realize
pages.head: "Difficult to see"

pages.span: selflessness in it? The "ground of the mind" is the three realms where the mind matures and wherever that mind moves by focusing on all phenomena. In both of those aspects, it is realizing the selflessness of persons and phenomena exactly as they truly are. "Very fine" means very difficult to realize; how it is fine was shown previously. Now it is shown by mentioning examples: "Just as a painting is drawn in the sky, and just as the wind stays in the expanse of space, so too here, the untainted primordial wisdom of the Blessed Ones is difficult to see when classified." This shows the following: for example, a painting drawn in the sky is not visible because it does not abide there as it does on a wall; and for example, the wind in the sky is not visible through its moving activity because it does not abide there like a leaf; yet it is not that those two do not occur in the sky. Likewise, the explanation, which is like the wind, and the drawing of a painting on the inexpressible reality, which is like the sky, are not visible because they are not of that nature; because they arise suddenly and do not abide there. However, it is not that they do not occur there. Thus, the primordial wisdom of the Buddha is divided into parts by the classifications of the explanation; although classified, it is difficult to see. In that regard, the drawing of the painting shows the collections of names, phrases, and letters, because it is the occasion of the explanation. The wind, which is the basis of sound, shows the words; those two are what is to be explained and what is to be heard. If one asks, "If it can be heard in any way, why not explain it even if it is difficult to see?" he said: "My mind thinks this: Who in the world will realize this? Since one who is clear-minded in this supreme matter is rare, I have no joy in explaining this." In that regard, "to realize" means to comprehend. "Clear-minded" means endowed with devotion. What does this show? If those endowed with the previously mentioned realization and devotion can hear this, they are rare in the world; therefore, he thinks, "I will not speak."
pages.head: How does one realize
